target_customer: Remote and distributed software teams doing pair programming and design review
problem: Existing screen sharing tools were built for one way presentations, so collaborators could not both point and type at once.
business_model: per user subscription starting at 11 dollars per month

founders.name: Jahanzeb Sherwani
founders.background_notes: Became Slack's Director of Realtime Communication Products after the deal; later founded Pop.

founders.background_notes: No bio on the YC page.

technical_complexity.rationale: Low latency multi cursor screen sharing with audio on Mac and Windows, built on WebRTC, needed real systems engineering from a small team.

defensibility.rationale: The second cursor idea was easy to explain and later copied into larger products; the lead was execution and latency.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Slack courted the company for seven months and bought it in January 2015; the feature was absorbed into Slack and Screenhero was retired.

market_need_then: Remote and pair work was growing among engineering teams; the founders built the product because they themselves wanted to work remotely together.

branding.domain_note: screenhero.com now redirects to Slack's huddles page.
branding.brand_signature: Each user gets their own cursor

rebrands.why: Screenhero was retired after migration into Slack, per TechCrunch coverage.

branding.community_and_virality: Widely written up by TechCrunch, The Next Web and Lifehacker at launch, and customers included GitHub and New Relic; Slack's built in version was later removed in 2019 per a CoScreen blog.

brand_strength.rationale: Memorable product demo and a clear name that drew solid launch press, but no merch or community found.

outcome_analysis: Screenhero built a collaborative screen sharing tool with a shared second cursor and gained customers like GitHub, New Relic and SendGrid. Slack CEO Stewart Butterfield approached the CEO in 2014 and the founders chose to join in January 2015 in a cash and stock deal of undisclosed size, so the outcome was a strategic technology acquisition that retired the standalone product.
notes: Funding unverified and conflicting: a Business Insider snippet says 2.6M from True Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz and Elad Gil; Crunchbase and CB Insights say about 1.8M over 5 rounds. The TechCrunch deal article did not state funding. Neither figure is recorded as a round. The YC page lists a team size of 2 but four founders; a search snippet says the founders earlier built iTeleport (not opened). Completeness pass: databases still conflict on total raised (ZoomInfo about 1.8M in one 2013 round; PitchBook 2.6M with Andreessen Horowitz; Crunchbase partial). No single dated amount is reliable, so no round is recorded and the total is a known gap.
